paragraphs.heading: Halfway gone
paragraphs.text: Half-life, written t_½, is the time it takes for a quantity to drop to half of what it started at. The term is often used in nuclear physics, where it describes how fast unstable atoms go through radioactive decay, or how long stable atoms last. It is also used more broadly for any exponential decay, and now and then for decay that is not exponential. Its mirror image is doubling time, which tracks growth by a factor of 2 instead of shrinking by that factor.

paragraphs.heading: Back to Rutherford
paragraphs.text: The first name for it, half-life period, dates back to 1907, when Ernest Rutherford discovered the principle. The name was trimmed to half-life in the early 1950s. Rutherford put the principle to work in dating rocks, by measuring how long radium takes to decay to lead-206.

paragraphs.heading: The same every time
paragraphs.text: For a quantity that decays exponentially, the half-life does not change over its whole lifetime. It serves as a characteristic unit for the exponential decay equation. It ties to the decay constant λ, a positive number, through t_(1/2) = (ln (2))/λ, where ln(2) is the natural logarithm of 2, roughly 0.693.

paragraphs.heading: Half-life for single atoms
paragraphs.text: Half-life often describes things that come in whole units, like radioactive atoms. With one atom whose half-life is one second, there cannot be half an atom left a second later. So the half-life is defined using probability: it is the time for exactly half of the atoms to decay on average, which means any one atom has a 50% chance of decaying within it. With a large number of identical atoms, the law of large numbers makes "half remain after one half-life" a very good approximation, though random variation keeps it from being exact.

paragraphs.heading: Half-lives in chemistry
paragraphs.text: In a chemical reaction, a substance's half-life is the time for its concentration to fall to half of where it began. In a first order reaction, the reaction rate is proportional to the concentration of the reactant, so the concentration falls exponentially. Its half-life, t_(1/2) = (ln 2)/k, does not depend on the starting concentration at all, only on the rate constant k. In a zero order reaction, by contrast, the concentration falls in a straight line, and the half-life depends on both the starting concentration and the rate constant.

paragraphs.heading: Inside the body
paragraphs.text: In medicine, people talk about the biological half-life of a drug or other chemical inside the human body. This is the time a substance, such as a drug or a radioactive nuclide, takes to lose half of its pharmacologic, physiologic or radiological activity. A radioactive isotope decays almost perfectly by first order kinetics, but a living body usually clears substances in a more complicated way. The biological half-life of water in a person is about 9 to 10 days, though behaviour and other conditions can change it, and for caesium it is between one and four months.
